ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Latin pipio Old French pyjonbor. Middle English pygeoun English pigeon Inherited from Middle English pygeoun, borrowed from Old French pyjon, inherited from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), derived from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”), of imitative origin. Partly displaced native English dove.
From pidgin English, from a Chinese Pidgin English pronunciation of English business during trade in the Far East. See pidgin.

senses.d: One of several birds of the family Columbidae within the order Columbiformes.
The meat from this bird.
A person who is a target or victim of a confidence game.
A pacifist, appeaser, an isolationist, a dove.
A person hired to transport film footage out of a region where transport options are limited.
ex: Kalb rushed to the airport and found a "pigeon" to take out the film: an American woman headed for London.

senses.d: A weak or useless person.
To deceive with a confidence game.
Concern or responsibility.

grp.label: bird of the dove and pigeon family Columbidae — see also dove

ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *-ōder. Proto-Indo-European *-Hōder.? Latin -ō Latin pipio Old French pyjon French pigeon Inherited from Old French pyjon, from Late Latin pīpiōnem (“chirping bird”), from Latin pīpiāre (“to chirp”).

it:piccione.gl: a pigeon; more accurately the rock pigeon, feral pigeon or domestic pigeon

ety.text: Borrowed from Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Doublet of pippione.
From Latin columbus.
Inherited from Old Spanish paloma, from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus, palumbēs (“wood pigeon”).

es:palomo.gl: male dove, male pigeon, cock pigeon

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish palomo, from Latin palumbus, from Proto-Indo-European *pal-wo- (“dark-colored, gray”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese *poombo, from Latin palumbus (“wood pigeon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pal-wo (“dark-colored, gray”). Cognate with Spanish paloma.

From Old Galician-Portuguese poomba (13th century: Cantigas de Santa Maria), from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese paomba, from Proto-Ibero-Romance palomba, from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus, from Proto-Indo-European *pal-wo (“dark-colored, gray”). Doublet of Paloma.

From Middle English pigge (“pig, piglet”) (originally a term for a young pig, with adult pigs being swyn (“swine”)), from Old English *picga, *pycga (attested in picgbrēad (“mast, pig-fodder”)), perhaps a diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *puk, *pūk (“pig”), which also gave rise to Middle Low German pûke, puyke (“pig, piglet”). Pokorny suggests this root might be somehow related to *bū-, *bew- (“to blow; swell”), which could account for the alternation between "pig" and "big".
Possibly a transferred use of pig, because the vessel was thought to resemble the animal.

senses.d: Any of several mammalian species of the family Suidae, having cloven hooves, bristles and a snout adapted for digging; especially the domesticated animal Sus domesticus.
ex: The man kept a pen with two pigs that he fed everything from carrots to cabbage.
[…]and at the back a rambling courtledge of barns and walls, around which pigs and bare-foot children grunted in loving communion of dirt.

senses.d: A young swine, a piglet (contrasted with a hog, an adult swine).
The edible meat of such an animal; pork.
ex: Some religions prohibit their adherents from eating pig.
"Miss Chastene, could you fetch me out an extra plate of pig and biscuit. My partner can't do without your marvelous cooking."

senses.d: A light pinkish-red colour, like that of a pig (also called piggy pink).
Someone who overeats or eats rapidly and noisily.
ex: You gluttonous pig! Now that you've eaten all the cupcakes, there will be none for the party!

senses.d: A lecherous or sexist man.
ex: She considered him a pig, as he invariably stared at her bosom when they talked.

senses.d: A dirty or slovenly person.
ex: He was a pig and his apartment a pigpen; take-away containers and pizza boxes in a long, moldy stream lined his counter tops.

senses.d: An obese person.
syn: All are derogatory unless otherwise labeled

senses.d: A police officer.
ex: The protester shouted, “Don't give in to the pigs!” as he was arrested.
There will be no pictures of pigs shooting down brothers on the instant replay

senses.d: A difficult problem.
ex: Hrm... this one's a real pig: I've been banging my head against the wall over it for hours!
Chewing-gum is a pig to get out of your hair.

senses.d: To give birth.
ex: The black sow pigged at seven this morning.

senses.d: To greedily consume (especially food).
ex: They were pigging on the free food at the bar.
"Wow, Doc. That's heavy." Denis sat there pigging on the joint as usual.

senses.d: To huddle or lie together like pigs, in one bed.
To live together in a crowded filthy manner.
To clean (a pipeline) using a pig (the device).
An earthenware pot or jar
An earthenware vessel used as a hot-water bottle

grp.label: someone who overeats or eats rapidly

ety.text: Originally imitative of the noise a pig makes.
Inherited from Middle French porc, from Old French porc, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”).
Inherited from Old French pourcel, purcel, from Late Latin porcellus, diminutive of Latin porcus.
From Latin maiālis, from the goddess Maia.
From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos.
Borrowed from Latin suinus.
From cerda + -o.

Borrowed from Middle French coche, from German Kutsche, from Hungarian kocsi, in reference to Kocs, a village in Hungary where the first horse-drawn vehicles with an innovative suspension system were manufactured in the 15th century. Doublet of coach.
Onomatopoeic.

pt:porco.gl: pig (the domesticated farm animal Sus scrofa)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese porco, from Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos (“young swine, young pig”). Compare Galician porco.
Learned borrowing from Latin suīnus.
From sale (“dirty”) + -aud.
From nojo (“disgust”) + -ento.
Inherited from Old French, from poule + -et.

From earlier flique, probably a borrowing of German Flick, German criminal slang for "young man". Alternatively, from earlier fligue, short for earlier fligman, a borrowing of German Fliege (“policeman”, literally “fly”). More at English fly.
Apocope of keufli, verlan form of flic (“cop”).
Proto-Indo-European *der-der. Proto-Germanic *teranąbor.? Vulgar Latin *tīrāre Spanish tirardeverb. Spanish tira Deverbal from tirar.
From choto + -a.

phr: as happy as a pig in mud
